description: We are a multidisciplinary team bridging computer science, bioinformatics, hardware, and health sciences to solve deep-space physiological degradation. Inspired by high-energy astrophysics, we combine custom sensor hardware and biological data to monitor cellular stress under cosmic radiation and microgravity, building functional telemetry devices, firmware, and computational intelligence for space exploration.
summary: Bio-Tesseract is a software-based health monitoring system for crews in isolated and extreme environments, where space radiation, microgravity, pressure variation and confinement act concurrently and ground medical support is delayed or unavailable. The system acquires synchronized multi-sensor telemetry (PPG, EMF, IMU, temperature, elevation, air quality, noise, vibration, humidity) and streams it to a centralized database. Incoming data is compared against benchmark-informed baselines drawn from NASA OSDR and ALSDA datasets. An ML model computes an entropy gap, defined as the normalized deviation between the Shannon entropy of a live sensor-feature window and that of the baseline, where larger gaps indicate greater loss of physiological regularity. It then identifies affected organ systems and grades severity. An LLM advisor converts the detected state and historical health data into onboard emergency guidance independent of ground control. A live dashboard presents readings, anomalies and system outputs in a single interface, and the full source code is available at Github. The project addresses the challenge by shifting from retrospective monitoring to organ-level, benchmark-anchored risk detection and decision support at the point of care. The modular architecture transfers to mine workers, deep-sea divers and high-altitude climbers. Planned extensions include ECG and SpO₂ integration, edge inference and an organ-level digital twin.
details:
What it does and how it works. Bio-Tesseract is a software-based monitoring and decision-support system for crews in isolated environments. Nine sensor modalities (PPG, EMF, IMU, temperature, elevation, air quality, acoustic noise, vibration, humidity) are acquired, filtered, timestamped and synchronized, then transmitted by live telemetry to a centralized database. Incoming data is compared against benchmark-informed baselines drawn from NASA OSDR and ALSDA datasets. The ML model computes an entropy gap, the normalized deviation between the Shannon entropy of a live sensor-feature window and that of the baseline, and uses it to identify affected organ systems and grade severity. An LLM advisor converts the detected state and historical health data into onboard emergency guidance that does not depend on ground control. Pulse-derived blood pressure and oxygen saturation estimates are calibrated to the individual’s BMI.

Benefits. The system gives early, organ-level risk detection rather than isolated vital-sign readings. It couples physiological and environmental exposure data in one framework. It also provides immediate decision support when communication with Earth is delayed, and it runs as software on commodity sensing hardware.

Intended impact. The project aims to make astronaut healthcare proactive and autonomous during long-duration missions. The modular architecture transfers to other extreme settings, including mining, deep-sea diving and high-altitude climbing, where immediate medical assistance is unavailable.

Tools, languages, hardware and software. Hardware: PPG, EMF, IMU, temperature, elevation, air-quality, acoustic, vibration and humidity sensors. Software: Programming Language: Python, JavaScript, R, TypeScript. ML libraries: scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost and SciPy and a web dashboard. Source code is at https://github.com/Hardik-Sharma-1005/Project-Bio-Tesseract. Reference data: NASA OSDR and ALSDA.

Creativity. The project’s contribution is integration. It anchors multi-sensor physiological and environmental telemetry to NASA benchmark datasets, maps deviations to organ-level and severity outputs through an entropy-based anomaly measure, and closes the loop with an LLM advisor that reasons over current and historical state. Existing wearables in the field monitor parameters; this system interprets them.

Factors considered. The design addresses five astronaut stressors together: space radiation, microgravity, pressure variation, isolation and delayed emergency care. The team reviewed existing wearable and astronaut-monitoring systems (Q-Naut, Bio-Monitor, Astroskin, EmbracePlus and others) to define the gap. Design constraints included individual calibration by BMI, modularity across environments, and autonomy from ground control. Radiation exposure is simulated in the current prototype, and ECG and SpO₂ sensing, personalized predictive models, edge inference, an organ-level digital twin and radiation-resilient hardware are planned extensions.
